title: New type of architecture for agentic memory
content:
Agentic Learning Without Retention
Authors/Creators
Description
We keep trying to build generalist agents by giving them more stuff (more memory, more skills, more tools); hoping all of that somehow turns them into better decision makers! But that doesn't really scale well, it's too much context for any type of intelligence.
The current structure is broken: save the conversation > summarize > retrieve > dig through thousands of MDs. Imagine if a human had to go to a library everytime he/she needed to make a decision. That system design worked for low to mid level tasks, but it will not work for high level decision making.
Most of those MDs are too specific, mixed with wrong assumptions, and a lot of noise. No intelligence should operate that way, not even if it had unlimited memory. Evolution figured that a long time ago & we should too.
A true generalist shouldn't need to remember every experience it had, or even know much about the domain it's working on. It shouldn't need to recall the actual knowlege, that can be outsourced cheaply. What the system needs to carry from one agent to the next is an understanding of why things failed.
This paper tried to formalize that approach. Instead of trying to retain domain experience; it figured out a good way to extract tiny high-level knowledge that works across different domains The agent doesn't need to remember how it solved a problem, It just needs to remember what not to do.
This paper proposes a new type of architecture for agentic memory:
- The active agent has many experiences, some in totally different domains. It picks the ones that failed not the one that were successful.
- A slow layer called LWR makes an assumption about the underlying mechanics of those failed runs.
- Then it tries to kill the assumption.
The assumptions that survive long enough gets used in forming general principles.
The principles that are backed by more than 1 assumption gets more attention.
The star principles are used to build a world model that get handed tp new agents.
The world model weakens with time.
The individual experiences are deleted completely
Failed Experiences → Assumptions → Refutation → Principles → World Model
Note: An additional perk of this type of structure; an agent's bias won't carry to other agents. Less proven assumptions die with time, so earlier bad assumptions won't carry. Humans suffer from that bias, agents shouldn't. An occational unproven assumption might be a game changer though, the agent would miss big on that. But that is where humans shine anyways, blind unstructure faith that flips the table once every blue moon. 2020s agents aim is self-improvement not self-reinvention anyways.

report.summary: A new preprint proposes LWR, an agent-memory architecture that discards raw experiences and retains only refuted assumptions distilled into a decaying world model.
report.background: Agent builders have largely scaled memory by adding more: longer context windows, conversation summaries, retrieval over notes, skill libraries and tool registries. That works for low- and mid-level tasks, but it creates noisy, over-specific context and does not reliably improve high-level decisions. The preprint 'Agentic Learning Without Retention,' posted on Zenodo with code on GitHub, argues that generalist agents should not hoard domain experience. Instead, they should extract compact, cross-domain lessons from failure and pass those forward. It proposes a slow LWR layer that forms assumptions about failed runs, tries to refute them, promotes survivors to principles, and builds a decaying world model. The work is conceptual and, at publication, lacks reported benchmark results, so it should be treated as a research direction rather than a validated replacement for existing memory systems.
key_points: Failure-first selection: instead of replaying successful trajectories, the active agent feeds failed experiences—including ones from unrelated domains—into the slow LWR layer. That layer hypothesizes why the failure happened and then actively tries to kill the hypothesis. Only assumptions that survive refutation become candidates for general principles. The design deliberately treats success as less informative than controlled failure.

Compression pipeline: the proposed flow is failed experiences → assumptions → refutation → principles → world model. Principles supported by multiple independent assumptions get more weight, and the resulting world model is handed to new agents. Raw experiences are deleted, and the world model decays over time so stale conclusions lose influence. This is memory as distilled priors, not a searchable archive.

Bias isolation: because individual experiences are deleted and unproven assumptions expire, one agent's bad assumptions should not silently propagate to successors. The paper frames this as an advantage over human-like memory, where early biases persist. The trade-off is explicit: a rare, unproven but transformative assumption may be discarded, and the authors concede that humans may be better at such blind, high-variance bets.

Outsource knowledge, retain prohibitions: the agent need not recall domain facts or even how it solved a problem; those can be retrieved cheaply. What it carries forward is 'what not to do.' This contrasts with current stacks that accumulate more memory, skills and tools in hopes of general intelligence. The claim is that compact negative knowledge transfers better across domains than detailed episodic recall.

Open validation questions: the preprint offers an architecture, not evidence. It does not report standard agent benchmarks, ablation studies, or comparisons with retrieval-based memory. Key unknowns include how to generate reliable refutations, represent and decay a world model, weight principles, and prevent the slow layer from becoming a new bias source. The GitHub repository may help others test the idea.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper is a useful counterweight to context-window and memory-database arms races: it argues that abstraction and negative knowledge, not volume, drive generalization. If validated, evaluation would need to measure transfer and failure avoidance, not just recall. For developers, it implies thinner memory stores, explicit deletion and decay policies, and a refutation pipeline that is harder to build than RAG. For users, agents could become more consistent across sessions and less likely to inherit stale assumptions, but also less personalized and prone to losing useful specifics. The lack of benchmarks means these benefits remain speculative.
report.tools: Start with the paper's GitHub repository (github.com/sshoman/lwr) for implementation details. Compare it with open-source memory layers such as Letta (MemGPT), Mem0, Zep, Cognee and LangGraph's memory/checkpointing patterns. Watch for benchmarks on cross-domain transfer, catastrophic forgetting and assumption-refutation reliability. A practical experiment: wrap a small agent in a failure-log → assumption → refutation loop and test whether distilled principles outperform retrieval over raw trajectories.
